name: Paleolithic cave art
what: Animals, hand stencils and hunting scenes painted and engraved on cave walls with ochre and charcoal.
why: The oldest surviving images: Sulawesi and western Europe show that figurative art appears among Homo sapiens on opposite sides of the world by 40,000 years ago.
spread: Not one spread but many independent starts: Indonesia, Iberia and France, India and Patagonia each have their own long traditions.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Megalithic monuments
what: Standing stones, stone circles and passage tombs raised without metal tools.
why: Göbekli Tepe shows hunter-gatherers building monuments before farming; Atlantic Europe later shared a megalithic culture from Iberia to Orkney.
spread: Göbekli Tepe stands alone in the Neolithic Levant; the European tradition seems to start in Brittany around 4500 BCE and travel by sea along the Atlantic coast.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Mesopotamian ziggurat and glazed brick
what: Stepped mud-brick temple platforms (ziggurats) and walls faced with glazed, moulded brick.
why: With no stone and little timber, Mesopotamia built monumentally in mud brick; its glazed-brick processional style passed to Persepolis and Susa.
spread: From Sumer (Uruk, Ur) north to Assyria and east to Elam (Chogha Zanbil), ending with Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Ancient Egyptian monumental
what: Dressed-stone pyramids and temples on an axis of pylons, courts and hypostyle halls, carved with hieroglyphic relief.
why: The first large-scale stone architecture in the world, and a style that stayed recognisably itself for nearly 3,000 years.
spread: Up and down the Nile from Memphis to Thebes and into Nubia; Greek and Roman rulers kept building in it (Philae, Edfu).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Kushite (Nubian) pyramids
what: Steep, small pyramids over royal tombs with offering chapels, built by the kings of Kush at Napata and Meroë.
why: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: about 200 at Meroë alone, built centuries after Egypt stopped.
spread: Kushite kings who ruled Egypt as the 25th dynasty revived the pyramid at El-Kurru and Nuri, and it moved south with the capital to Meroë.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Aegean Bronze Age palaces
what: Minoan palace complexes with light wells and frescoes, then Mycenaean citadels of huge "Cyclopean" blocks and corbelled tholos tombs.
why: Europe's first palace architecture; it vanished in the Late Bronze Age collapse.
spread: From Crete to the Greek mainland after about 1450 BCE, when Mycenaeans took over Knossos.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Achaemenid Persian
what: Columned audience halls (apadana) with bull-headed capitals on stone terraces, and processions of tribute bearers in relief.
why: A deliberately imperial style: Darius's Susa charter boasts that Ionian, Lydian, Egyptian and Babylonian craftsmen built it together.
spread: From Pasargadae to Persepolis and Susa; Ashoka's polished pillars in India probably borrow from it.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Sasanian Persian
what: Rubble-and-mortar domes on squinches and huge vaulted open halls (iwans), with royal rock reliefs.
why: The iwan and the squinch dome became the backbone of Islamic architecture in Iran and beyond.
spread: From Ardashir's palace at Firuzabad to the Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon; after 651 the forms passed straight to Islamic builders.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Greek temple and the classical orders
what: Stone temples ringed with columns in the Doric and Ionic orders, built to fixed proportions, with sculpted pediments.
why: The orders became the grammar of Western architecture for 2,500 years, from Rome to the US Capitol.
spread: Across Greek colonies from Sicily (Agrigento, Paestum) to Ionia (Ephesus, Didyma).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Hellenistic
what: Bigger, more theatrical Greek building and sculpture: Corinthian columns, colossal statues, sculpture in motion.
why: Alexander's conquests carried Greek forms from Egypt to Afghanistan, where they later met Buddhism.
spread: Alexandria, Pergamon, Rhodes and Antioch were the centres; Ai-Khanoum on the Oxus was a Greek city with a gymnasium and theatre.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Roman arch, vault and concrete
what: Arches, barrel and groin vaults and domes in Roman concrete, wrapped in Greek orders as decoration.
why: Concrete let Rome enclose huge interior spaces; the Pantheon's 43 m dome was the largest for 1,300 years.
spread: Built across the empire on one model: forum, baths, amphitheatre, aqueduct, from Britain to Syria.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Indus brick cities
what: Grid-planned cities of standard-sized baked brick, with covered drains, granaries and public baths.
why: Urban planning at a scale nobody else had in 2500 BCE, and almost no palaces or temples.
spread: Over a million square km from Harappa to Gujarat (Dholavira, Lothal).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Buddhist stupa, cave and pagoda
what: Domed relic mounds (stupas) with carved gateways, rock-cut cave halls, and the stupa stretched upward into the pagoda.
why: The stupa travelled with monks and became the tiered pagoda of China, Korea and Japan and the terraced mandala of Borobudur.
spread: Ashoka spread stupas across India; monks and merchants carried the form along the Silk Road to China (Mogao, 366) and by sea to Java.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Gandhara Greco-Buddhist art
what: Buddhist sculpture in grey schist and stucco with Greek drapery, contrapposto and Apollo-like faces.
why: Among the first images of the Buddha as a man; the type travelled to Central Asia and China.
spread: Under the Kushans from Taxila and Peshawar into Afghanistan (Bamiyan) and along the Silk Road.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Hindu temple (Nagara and Dravida)
what: A dark sanctum (garbhagriha) under a tower: the curving shikhara in the north (Nagara), the stepped vimana and gateway gopurams in the south (Dravida).
why: The temple as a model of the cosmic mountain; the plan travelled to Java and Cambodia.
spread: From Gupta stone temples to the Chalukyas, Pallavas and Cholas; traders and Brahmins carried it to Southeast Asia (Prambanan, Angkor).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Indo-Islamic and Mughal
what: Persian domes, iwans and charbagh gardens built in red sandstone and white marble with Indian brackets, chhatris and inlay (pietra dura).
why: A fusion style that produced the Taj Mahal and later fed British Indo-Saracenic building.
spread: From the Delhi Sultanate (Qutb Minar) to the Mughal capitals Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Delhi and Lahore.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Chinese imperial timber and tomb art
what: Timber halls on stone platforms whose roofs ride on interlocking bracket sets (dougong), laid out on axial courtyards; and imperial tombs filled with sculpture.
why: One system scaled from house to palace; written down in the Yingzao Fashi (1103) and copied across Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
spread: From the Qin and Han capitals through Tang Chang'an, the model for Nara and Kyoto, to the Ming Forbidden City.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Japanese temple, shrine and castle
what: Chinese-derived Buddhist halls and pagodas, unpainted Shinto shrines rebuilt in cycles, and later white-plastered castles.
why: Holds the world's oldest surviving wooden buildings (Horyu-ji) and the Ise practice of rebuilding the same shrine every 20 years.
spread: Arrived with Buddhism from Korea and China; Nara and Kyoto copied Chang'an's grid.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Khmer temple-mountain
what: Stepped sandstone pyramids with five towers standing for Mount Meru, inside moats, carved with narrative reliefs.
why: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument on earth; the temples sat in a hydraulic city of perhaps 750,000 people.
spread: From Roluos (Bakong, 881) to Angkor; the style reached Thailand (Phimai) and outlived the empire in Thai prangs.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Early Islamic (Umayyad and Abbasid)
what: Hypostyle mosques with courtyards, the mihrab and minaret, mosaics and arabesque, borrowing Byzantine and Sasanian craftsmen.
why: Set the plan of the congregational mosque used from Spain to Central Asia.
spread: Umayyad Damascus to Córdoba; Abbasid Baghdad and Samarra to Ibn Tulun's Cairo and Kairouan.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Moorish (al-Andalus and the Maghreb)
what: Horseshoe and polylobed arches, carved stucco, muqarnas and tiled courts with water.
why: Spain's Islamic centuries left the Alhambra and a Mudéjar style Christian kings kept using.
spread: Córdoba to Seville, Marrakesh, Fez and Granada; Mudéjar carried it into Christian Spain and then to Latin America.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Persian Islamic (Seljuk to Safavid)
what: Four-iwan mosques, double-shell domes on tall drums, and whole surfaces in glazed tile mosaic.
why: The tiled blue dome of Samarkand and Isfahan is Iran's gift to the Islamic world, from Istanbul to Agra.
spread: Seljuk Isfahan to Ilkhanid Soltaniyeh, Timurid Samarkand and Herat, Safavid Isfahan.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Ottoman imperial mosque
what: A central dome over a square, buttressed by half-domes, with pencil minarets and Iznik tile.
why: Sinan answered Hagia Sophia: the Selimiye's dome finally matched it in size, in a lighter structure.
spread: From Bursa and Edirne to Istanbul, then out to Cairo, Damascus, Sarajevo and Algiers.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Sudano-Sahelian mud-brick
what: Mosques of sun-dried mud brick over timber, with protruding wooden beams (toron) used as scaffolding for yearly replastering.
why: Living buildings: the Great Mosque of Djenné is re-plastered by the whole town every year.
spread: Along the Niger trade cities of Mali and Songhai (Timbuktu, Djenné, Gao) and out to Agadez and northern Ghana.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Swahili coral stone
what: Mosques, palaces and tombs of coral rag and lime with domes and vaults, in Indian Ocean port towns.
why: Kilwa's Husuni Kubwa was the largest building south of the Sahara in its day, paid for by Zimbabwe gold.
spread: Up and down the East African coast from Mogadishu to Kilwa, tied to Arabia, Persia and India by the monsoon.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Byzantine domed church
what: Domes on pendentives over centralised plans, gold-ground mosaics and icons.
why: Hagia Sophia set the problem of the great dome that Ottoman and Renaissance builders kept answering.
spread: Ravenna and Venice in the west, Kyiv and Novgorod in the north, the Balkans and Armenia-Georgia in the east.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Russian Orthodox (onion domes, tented roofs)
what: Byzantine cross-in-square churches turned upward: bulbous onion domes, tented roofs, timber churches and icon screens.
why: A Byzantine import that became a national style, and in timber the most intricate wooden churches anywhere.
spread: From Kyiv and Novgorod to Vladimir and then Moscow, which claimed the Byzantine mantle after 1453.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Romanesque
what: Thick walls, round arches, barrel and groin vaults, and small windows: monastic and pilgrimage churches.
why: Europe's first shared style since Rome; the monk Raoul Glaber wrote of a "white mantle of churches" after 1000.
spread: Carried by the Cluniac monks and the pilgrimage road to Santiago; the Normans took it to England and Sicily.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Gothic
what: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses that take the load off the walls so they can be glass.
why: The structural trick that turned churches into lanterns of stained glass, from Abbot Suger's choir onward.
spread: From the Paris basin across Latin Europe within a century; Brick Gothic on the Baltic, Perpendicular in England, Flamboyant in France.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Ethiopian highland (Aksumite stelae and rock-hewn churches)
what: Granite stelae carved as multi-storey towers, then whole churches cut down into living rock.
why: Aksum's stelae are among the largest single stones ever raised; Lalibela's churches were carved, not built.
spread: From Aksum to the Zagwe capital at Lalibela and the later royal city of Gondar.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Southern African dry-stone (Zimbabwe tradition)
what: Curving granite walls laid without mortar, enclosing royal compounds on hilltops and valleys.
why: Great Zimbabwe's walls rise 11 m; colonial writers refused to credit it to Africans, and that lie had to be dismantled.
spread: From Mapungubwe to Great Zimbabwe, then Khami and Danangombe as power shifted west.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Renaissance
what: Roman orders, round arches and domes in clear mathematical proportion, and painting built on linear perspective.
why: Florence rebuilt antiquity on purpose; the result became the default language of European building and art.
spread: Florence to Rome by 1500; then France (Chambord), Spain (El Escorial), Poland and Russia via Italian architects.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Baroque and Rococo
what: Curving facades, oval plans, light from hidden windows, illusionistic ceilings: architecture as theatre.
why: The Counter-Reformation's style for moving the faithful, then the absolutist palace style of Versailles.
spread: Rome to Catholic Europe and Spanish and Portuguese America, which made it its own; Rococo lightened it in 18th-century Germany and France.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Neoclassical
what: Strict Greek and Roman temple forms, plain surfaces and colonnades, after the digs at Pompeii and the study of Greek ruins.
why: The style of the Enlightenment and the new republics: Washington's Capitol and Paris's Panthéon.
spread: From Rome and Paris to Berlin, St Petersburg, London and the United States; Napoleon's Empire style was its imperial turn.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Mesoamerican pyramid and plaza
what: Stepped pyramids crowned by temples around plazas and ballcourts, laid out on astronomical alignments.
why: Built with no draft animals, wheels or metal tools; Teotihuacan was one of the largest cities on earth around 500.
spread: Olmec to Maya, Zapotec and Teotihuacan; Toltec and Maya at Chichen Itza; Aztec Tenochtitlan.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Andean stone (Chavín to Inca)
what: Platform temples, adobe cities and finally Inca ashlar: polygonal blocks fitted without mortar, earthquake-proof.
why: Inca walls still stand in Cusco where Spanish buildings on top of them fell in earthquakes.
spread: Chavín and Tiwanaku, Chimú adobe at Chan Chan, then the Inca road network carried one imperial style 4,000 km.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Ancestral Puebloan great houses
what: Multi-storey masonry "great houses" with hundreds of rooms and round kivas, and cliff dwellings under rock overhangs.
why: Pueblo Bonito was the largest building in North America until the 1880s.
spread: Chaco Canyon was the hub of a road network; after drought around 1130 people moved to Mesa Verde, then south to the Rio Grande.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Mississippian mound cities
what: Flat-topped earthen platform mounds around plazas, carrying temples and chiefs' houses.
why: Cahokia's Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas; the city may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100.
spread: From the American Bottom near St Louis down the Mississippi and across the Southeast (Moundville, Etowah).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Rapa Nui moai
what: Nearly 1,000 monolithic figures of ancestors carved from volcanic tuff and set on stone platforms facing inland.
why: The most isolated inhabited island built some of the Pacific's largest monuments; the "ecocide" story is now disputed.
spread: Carved at one quarry, Rano Raraku, and moved upright ("walked") to platforms around the island.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Gothic Revival
what: Pointed arches, spires and tracery again, now on parliaments, universities, railway stations and early skyscrapers.
why: Romantic and religious nostalgia turned into the style of British imperial civic building.
spread: Britain to the colonies (Mumbai, Melbourne, Ottawa), Germany (finishing Cologne) and America (the Woolworth Building).

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Beaux-Arts and imperial eclecticism
what: Lavish symmetrical classical buildings taught at the École des Beaux-Arts, and colonial mixes like Indo-Saracenic.
why: The look of the confident 19th-century state: opera houses, stations, museums and viceroys' palaces.
spread: Paris trained architects from New York to Buenos Aires; the British mixed it with Mughal forms in India.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Art Nouveau
what: Whiplash curves, plant forms, iron and glass, with the building, furniture and ironwork designed as one.
why: The first international style to refuse historical copying, two decades before modernism.
spread: Brussels and Paris to Barcelona (Modernisme), Vienna (Secession), Glasgow, Prague and Riga.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Art Deco
what: Geometric ornament, zigzags and sunbursts, streamlined setbacks, chrome and terrazzo: modern glamour.
why: The skyscraper style of the 1920s and 1930s, and the city style of Mumbai, Shanghai and Miami Beach.
spread: Named after the 1925 Paris exposition; New York, Shanghai, Mumbai, Napier and Havana built whole districts in it.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Modernism and the International Style
what: Steel, glass and concrete, flat roofs, open plans and no ornament: form follows function.
why: The Bauhaus and Le Corbusier made it the world's default city style; Brasília and Chandigarh were built from scratch in it.
spread: Germany, France and the Netherlands to the US (émigré Bauhaus teachers), Latin America, India and the Soviet bloc.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Postmodern, high-tech and parametric
what: Exposed structure (high-tech), playful historical quotes (postmodern), and computer-designed curves (deconstructivist, parametric).
why: Signature buildings became tools of city branding: the "Bilbao effect".
spread: London and Paris to the Gulf and China, which built most of the world's supertall towers after 2000.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Chinese ink landscape (shanshui)
what: Monumental mountains and water in ink on silk and paper, seen from shifting viewpoints, tied to poetry and calligraphy.
why: For a thousand years China's highest art form, painted by scholar-officials rather than craftsmen.
spread: Northern Song court at Kaifeng, Southern Song Hangzhou, Yuan literati; to Korea and Japan (Sesshū), and into Persian painting via the Mongols.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Persian and Mughal miniature
what: Small, jewel-coloured book paintings for epics and histories, with high horizons and patterned space.
why: Born when Mongol rule brought Chinese painting to Iran; it shaped Ottoman and Mughal court art.
spread: Ilkhanid Tabriz to Timurid Herat (Behzad), Safavid Tabriz, then Mughal Delhi and Ottoman Istanbul.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints
what: Cheap colour woodblock prints of actors, courtesans, landscapes and the "floating world" of Edo.
why: Mass art for townspeople; when it reached Paris it rewired Monet, Van Gogh and Art Nouveau.
spread: Edo publishers; exported (often as packing paper) after 1854, sparking "Japonisme" in Europe.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Impressionism and Post-Impressionism
what: Painting outdoors in broken colour to catch light and moment, then pushed toward structure (Cézanne) and expression (Van Gogh).
why: Broke the Academy's hold and opened the road to modern art.
spread: Paris and its suburbs; to London, America, Russia and Japan by 1900.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Avant-garde (Cubism to abstraction)
what: Cubism, abstraction, Dada and Surrealism: art about seeing and about art itself.
why: Within a decade painting went from Picasso's broken faces to pure abstraction.
spread: Paris, Munich, Moscow and Zurich; after 1940 New York took over.

sources.note: Art and architecture workstream: written from general knowledge, check against this article

name: Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin bronze
what: Lost-wax cast bronze and brass: Igbo-Ukwu's ritual vessels, Ife's naturalistic heads, Benin's court plaques.
why: Technically among the finest metal casting anywhere; most Benin pieces were looted by Britain in 1897.
spread: Igbo-Ukwu (9th century), Ife (12th-15th), then the Benin court guild under the obas.
